desc_content.paragraph: builds(target, *args, **kw) returns a Hydra-compatible config that, when instantiated, returns target(*args, **kw).
I.e., instantiate(builds(target, *args, **kw)) == target(*args, **kw)
Consult the Notes section for more details, and the Examples section to see the various features of builds in action.

definition.paragraph: The target object to be configured. This is a required, positional-only argument.
Positional arguments passed as <hydra_target>(*pos_args, ...) upon instantiation.
Arguments specified positionally are not included in the config’s signature and are stored as a tuple bound to in the _args_ field.
The keyword arguments passed as <hydra_target>(..., **kwargs_for_target) upon instantiation.
The arguments specified here determine the signature of the resulting config, unless populate_full_signature=True is specified (see below).
Named parameters of the forms that have the prefixes hydra_, zen_ or _zen_ are reserved to ensure future-compatibility, and thus cannot be specified by the user.
If True, then the resulting config will instantiate as functools.partial(<hydra_target>, *pos_args, **kwargs_for_target). Thus this enables the partial-configuration of objects.

Specifying zen_partial=True and populate_full_signature=True together will populate the config’s signature only with parameters that: are explicitly specified by the user, or that have default values specified in the target’s signature. I.e. it is presumed that un-specified parameters that have no default values are to be excluded from the config.

definition_list_item.classifier: None | Callable | Builds | InterpStr | Sequence[None | Callable | Builds | InterpStr]

definition.paragraph: One or more wrappers, which will wrap hydra_target prior to instantiation. E.g. specifying the wrappers [f1, f2, f3] will instantiate as:
Wrappers can also be specified as interpolated strings [2] or targeted configs.
Specifies field-names and corresponding values that will be included in the resulting config, but that will not be used to instantiate <hydra_target>. These are called “meta” fields.
If True, then the resulting config’s signature and fields will be populated according to the signature of <hydra_target>; values also specified in **kwargs_for_target take precedent.
This option is not available for objects with inaccessible signatures, such as NumPy’s various ufuncs.
Specifies parameter names and/or indices, or a function for checking names, to exclude those parameters from the config-creation process.

term.strong: Note that inherited fields cannot be excluded.

definition.paragraph: A dictionary that modifies hydra-zen’s value and type conversion behavior. Consists of the following optional key-value pairs (hydra_zen.typing.ZenConvert):

If True any dataclass type/instance without a _target_ field is automatically converted to a targeted config that will instantiate to that type/instance. Otherwise the dataclass type/instance will be passed through as-is.
If True (default), builds(builds(f)) is equivalent to builds(f). I.e. the second builds call will use the _target_ field of its input, if it exists.
Specifies a tuple of parent classes that the resulting config inherits from.
If True, then Hydra will recursively instantiate all other hydra-config objects nested within this config [3].
If None, the _recursive_ attribute is not set on the resulting config.
Determines how Hydra handles the non-primitive, omegaconf-specific objects passed to <hydra_target> [4].

list_item.paragraph: "none": No conversion occurs; omegaconf containers are passed through (Default)
"partial": DictConfig and ListConfig objects converted to dict and

definition.paragraph: list, respectively. Structured configs and their fields are passed without conversion. - "all": All passed objects are converted to dicts, lists, and primitives, without a trace of OmegaConf containers. - "object": Passed objects are converted to dict and list. Structured Configs are converted to instances of the backing dataclass / attr class.
If None, the _convert_ attribute is not set on the resulting config.

definition_list_item.classifier: None | list[str | dict[str, str | list[str] | None ]], optional (default = None)

definition.paragraph: A list in an input config that instructs Hydra how to build the output config [6] [7]. Each input config can have a Defaults List as a top level element. The Defaults List itself is not a part of output config.
A dictionary that can specify any option that is supported by dataclasses.make_dataclass() other than fields. The default value for unsafe_hash is True.
target can be specified as a string to override the _target_ field set on the dataclass type returned by builds.
The module field can be specified to enable pickle compatibility. See hydra_zen.typing.DataclassOptions for details.

versionmodified.paragraph: Deprecated since version 0.9.0: frozen will be removed in hydra-zen 0.10.0. It is replaced by zen_dataclass={'frozen': <bool>}.

definition.paragraph: If True, the resulting config will create frozen (i.e. immutable) instances. I.e. setting/deleting an attribute of an instance will raise dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError at runtime.

versionmodified.paragraph: Deprecated since version 0.9.0: dataclass_name will be removed in hydra-zen 0.10.0. It is replaced by zen_dataclass={'cls_name': <str>}.

definition.paragraph: If specified, determines the name of the returned class object.
A dynamically-generated structured config (i.e. a dataclass type) that describes how to build hydra_target.
The provided configured value cannot be serialized by Hydra, nor does hydra-zen provide specialized support for it. See Configuration-Value Types Supported by Hydra and hydra-zen for more details.
Instantiates a configuration created by builds, returning the instantiated target.
Returns a new builds function with customized default values.
Creates a general config with customized field names, default values, and annotations.
Returns the target-object from a targeted structured config.
Produces a config that, when instantiated by Hydra, “just” returns the un-instantiated target-object.
Serialize a config as a yaml-formatted string.

desc_content.paragraph: The following pseudo code conveys the core functionality of builds:
desc_content.literal_block:
from dataclasses import make_dataclass
def builds(self,target, populate_full_signature=False, **kw): # Dynamically defines a Hydra-compatible dataclass type. # Akin to doing: # # @dataclass # class Builds_thing: # _target_: str = get_import_path(target) # # etc.
_target_ = get_import_path(target)
if populate_full_signature: sig = get_signature(target) kw = {**sig, **kw} # merge w/ preference for kw
type_annots = [get_hints(target)[k] for k in kw]
fields = [("_target_", str, _target_)] fields += [ ( field_name, hydra_compat_type_annot(hint), hydra_compat_val(v), ) for hint, (field_name, v) in zip(type_annots, kw.items()) ]
Config = make_dataclass(f"Builds_{target}", fields) return Config
desc_content.paragraph: The resulting “config” is a dynamically-generated dataclass type [5] with Hydra-specific attributes attached to it [1]. It possesses a _target_ attribute that indicates the import path to the configured target as a string.

Using any of the zen_xx features will result in a config that depends explicitly on hydra-zen. I.e. hydra-zen must be installed in order to instantiate the resulting config, including its yaml version.
For details of the annotation SupportedPrimitive, see Configuration-Value Types Supported by Hydra and hydra-zen.

Type annotations are inferred from the target’s signature and are only retained if they are compatible with Hydra’s limited set of supported annotations; otherwise an annotation is automatically ‘broadened’ until it is made compatible with Hydra.
builds provides runtime validation of user-specified arguments against the target’s signature. E.g. specifying mis-named arguments or too many arguments will cause builds to raise.
These examples describe:
A helpful utility for printing examples
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> from hydra_zen import builds, instantiate, to_yaml >>> def pyaml(x): ... # for pretty printing configs ... print(to_yaml(x))
desc_content.paragraph: Lets create a basic config that describes how to ‘build’ a particular dictionary.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> Conf = builds(dict, a=1, b='x')
desc_content.paragraph: The resulting config is a dataclass with the following signature and attributes:
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> Conf # signature: Conf(a: Any = 1, b: Any = 'x') <class 'types.Builds_dict'>
>>> pyaml(Conf) _target_: builtins.dict a: 1 b: x
desc_content.paragraph: The instantiate function is used to enact this build – to create the dictionary.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> instantiate(Conf) # calls: `dict(a=1, b='x')` {'a': 1, 'b': 'x'}
desc_content.paragraph: The default parameters that we provided can be overridden.
Positional arguments are supported.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> Conf = builds(len, [1, 2, 3]) >>> Conf._args_ # type: ignore [1, 2, 3] >>> instantiate(Conf) 3
desc_content.paragraph: builds can be used to partially-configure a target. Let’s create a config for the following function
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> def a_two_tuple(x: int, y: float): return x, y
desc_content.paragraph: such that we only configure the parameter x.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> PartialConf = builds(a_two_tuple, x=1, zen_partial=True) # configures only `x` >>> pyaml(PartialConf) _target_: __main__.a_two_tuple _partial_: true x: 1
desc_content.paragraph: Instantiating this config will return functools.partial(a_two_tuple, x=1).
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> partial_func = instantiate(PartialConf) >>> partial_func functools.partial(<function a_two_tuple at 0x00000220A7820EE0>, x=1)
desc_content.paragraph: And thus the remaining parameter can be provided post-instantiation.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> partial_func(y=22.0) # providing the remaining parameter (1, 22.0)
desc_content.paragraph: The configurable parameters of a target can be auto-populated in our config. Suppose we want to configure the following function.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> def bar(x: bool, y: str = 'foo'): return x, y
desc_content.paragraph: The following config will have a signature that matches bar; the annotations and default values of the parameters of bar are explicitly incorporated into the config.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> # signature: `Builds_bar(x: bool, y: str = 'foo')` >>> Conf = builds(bar, populate_full_signature=True) >>> pyaml(Conf) _target_: __main__.bar x: ??? 'y': foo
desc_content.paragraph: zen_exclude can be used to name parameter to be excluded from the auto-population process:
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> Conf2 = builds(bar, populate_full_signature=True, zen_exclude=["y"]) >>> pyaml(Conf2) _target_: __main__.bar x: ???
desc_content.paragraph: to exclude parameters by index:
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> Conf2 = builds(bar, populate_full_signature=True, zen_exclude=[-1]) >>> pyaml(Conf2) _target_: __main__.bar x: ???
desc_content.paragraph: or to specify a pattern - via a function - for excluding parameters:
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> Conf3 = builds(bar, populate_full_signature=True, ... zen_exclude=lambda name: name.startswith("x")) >>> pyaml(Conf3) _target_: __main__.bar 'y': foo
desc_content.paragraph: Annotations will be used by Hydra to provide limited runtime type-checking during instantiation. Here, we’ll pass a float for x, which expects a boolean value.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> instantiate(Conf(x=10.0)) # type: ignore ValidationError: Value '10.0' is not a valid bool (type float) full_key: x object_type=Builds_func
desc_content.paragraph: Because a config produced via builds is simply a class-object, we can compose configs via class inheritance.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> ParentConf = builds(dict, a=1, b=2) >>> ChildConf = builds(dict, b=-2, c=-3, builds_bases=(ParentConf,)) >>> instantiate(ChildConf) {'a': 1, 'b': -2, 'c': -3} >>> issubclass(ChildConf, ParentConf) # type: ignore True
desc_content.paragraph: Misspelled parameter names and other invalid configurations for the target’s signature will be caught by builds so that such errors are caught prior to instantiation.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> def func(a_number: int): pass
>>> builds(func, a_nmbr=2) # misspelled parameter name TypeError: Building: func ..
>>> builds(func, 1, 2) # too many arguments TypeError: Building: func ..
>>> BaseConf = builds(func, a_number=2) >>> builds(func, 1, builds_bases=(BaseConf,)) # too many args (via inheritance) TypeError: Building: func ..
>>> # value type not supported by Hydra >>> builds(int, (i for i in range(10))) # type: ignore hydra_zen.errors.HydraZenUnsupportedPrimitiveError: Building: int ..
desc_content.paragraph: Meta-fields are fields that are included in a config but are excluded by the instantiation process. Thus arbitrary metadata can be attached to a config.
Let’s create a config whose fields reference a meta-field via relative-interpolation [2].
Zen-wrappers enables us to make arbitrary changes to <hydra_target>, its inputs, and/or its outputs during the instantiation process.

Let’s use a wrapper to add a unit-conversion step to a config. We’ll modify a config that builds a function, which converts a temperature in Fahrenheit to Celsius, and add a wrapper to it so that it will convert from Fahrenheit to Kelvin instead.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> def faren_to_celsius(temp_f): # our target ... return ((temp_f - 32) * 5) / 9
>>> def change_celcius_to_kelvin(celc_func): # our wrapper ... def wraps(*args, **kwargs): ... return 273.15 + celc_func(*args, **kwargs) ... return wraps

>>> AsCelcius = builds(faren_to_celsius) >>> AsKelvin = builds(faren_to_celsius, zen_wrappers=change_celcius_to_kelvin) >>> instantiate(AsCelcius, temp_f=32) 0.0 >>> instantiate(AsKelvin, temp_f=32) 273.15
desc_content.paragraph: The dynamically-generated classes created by builds can be made pickle-compatible by specifying the name of the symbol that it is assigned to and the module in which it was defined.
desc_content.literal_block:
# contents of mylib/foo.py from pickle import dumps, loads
DictConf = builds(dict, zen_dataclass={'module': 'mylib.foo', 'cls_name': 'DictConf'})
assert DictConf is loads(dumps(DictConf))
desc_content.paragraph: Let’s create a config object whose instances will by “frozen” (i.e., immutable).
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> RouterConfig = builds(dict, ip_address=None, zen_dataclass={'frozen': True}) >>> my_router = RouterConfig(ip_address="192.168.56.1") # an immutable instance
desc_content.paragraph: Attempting to overwrite the attributes of my_router will raise.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> my_router.ip_address = "148.109.37.2" FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'ip_address'
desc_content.paragraph: Specifying builds(functools.partial(<target>, ...), ...) is supported; builds will automatically “unpack” a partial’d object that is passed as its target.
desc_content.doctest_block: >>> import functools >>> partiald_dict = functools.partial(dict, a=1, b=2) >>> Conf = builds(partiald_dict) # signature: (a = 1, b = 2) >>> instantiate(Conf) # equivalent to calling: `partiald_dict()` {'a': 1, 'b': 2} >>> instantiate(Conf(a=-4)) # equivalent to calling: `partiald_dict(a=-4)` {'a': -4, 'b': 2}
